addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- docs-consistency-guard: Documentation agent that audits docs for staleness and inconsistency AND generates/updates documentation on request. Use proactively when reviewing any PR that touches CLAUDE.md, docs/adr/, CONTRIBUTING.md, or docs/architecture.md. Also invoke when the user asks "is the documentation up to date?", "update the milestone", "scaffold the ADR for X", "add this to the ADR index", "add a TODO item", "scaffold a README for X", or "create a doc stub for Y." (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write, Edit)

- driver-boundary-guard: Specialized reviewer for values that cross a DRIVER boundary — anything DataQ receives from a database connector, pyiceberg, pandas/pyarrow, or a cloud SDK and then type-narrows (isinstance / dtype checks / hasattr). Audits whether the covering tests hand-build the value in the shape our model expects (the "fixture encodes our model" defect that hid (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>

Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>

<example>

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- qa-verifier: QA/QE agent that (1) runs the full local verification battery mirroring CI's required checks before any commit/push/PR, (2) audits test quality on changed code — failure-mode coverage, mocked-seam smells, coverage on changed files (Week-8 ≥80% gate), and (3) exercises the running application with data-level scenarios — authoring suites/checks through the real API, negative and edge-case inputs, authz probes — against the local stack's seeded demo data. Use proactively before pushing a branch or opening a PR, after writing or modifying tests, or when the user asks "run the gate", "is this ready to push?", "is this tested enough?", or "smoke the app with bad data". (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- regression-mutation-verifier: Proves that a new regression test actually fails against the unfixed code. Reverts the fix inside a throwaway git worktree, runs only the new test, and reports whether it fails for the RIGHT reason — catching tests that pass no matter what (the (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Edit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- ui-tester: End-to-end UI QA agent that exercises DataQ's frontend on BOTH desktop and mobile viewports (functionality + rendering) against the running app, AND audits backend↔frontend feature parity — flagging backend capabilities with no frontend surface (and frontend calls with no backend). ## claude.ai Microsoft Learn
# Microsoft Learn MCP Server

This server gives structured access to official Microsoft and Azure documentation via three tools:

## Tools

### microsoft_docs_search
Search official documentation and return up to 10 concise, high-quality content chunks (max 500 tokens each), including title, URL, and excerpt.

- Use first to get a quick, reliable overview
- Ideal for grounding answers in Microsoft knowledge

### microsoft_code_sample_search
Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn documentation and return up to 20 relevant, high-quality code samples.

- Use when you need to provide sample Microsoft/Azure related code in your answers.  
- Ideal for generating code snippets or practical implementation examples.  
- Optional parameter `language` can filter results. 

### microsoft_docs_fetch
Fetch and convert full Microsoft documentation pages to markdown.

- Use after search when you need full content from a specific URL
- Required for detailed tutorials, troubleshooting, prerequisites, code samples, or when search results are incomplete or outdated

## Workflow

1. Use `microsoft_docs_search` to find relevant documents.
2. If you need code examples or practical snippets, use `microsoft_code_sample_search`.
3. If deeper or complete information is needed, use `microsoft_docs_fetch`.

**Search gives breadth. Code Sample Search gives practical examples. Fetch gives depth.**

All content comes from Microsoft Learn or official sources, returned in clean markdown format.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

---

description: "Where things stand as of 2026-07-28 — OpenTofu migration + state encryption shipped and applied to prod, 3 P1s closed, Batches 2-4 scoped but not started, and the traps that session hit"

  node_type: memory

  originSessionId: 3577d6f5-2e75-42b2-a327-294abe25939e

---

Resume state as of **2026-07-28**. Overwrite this whole file at the next handover — it is
resume state, not history. Durable records live in the repo: `docs/progress.md` (per-PR
ledger) and `docs/ops-log.md` (harness lifecycle + credential rotation).

**State:** `main` = `b76a73ee`. 1 open PR (#1096). **32** open in the `v1.1 Backlog`
milestone, **58** repo-wide. Prod app stack was **applied and verified this session** —
post-apply `tofu plan` → `detailed_exitcode=0, No changes`; frontend 200 / `/healthz` ok /
`/api/v1/runs` 401.

## Do these first

1. **Copy the OpenTofu state passphrase off this machine.** `state_encryption_passphrase`
   in the gitignored `deploy/terraform/azure/terraform.tfvars`. It is a **data-at-rest key,
   not a credential** — it cannot be revoked or re-minted, and losing it makes
   `terraform.tfstate` unrecoverable. **Plaintext state backups are deliberately RETAINED**
   until that copy exists (user: "keep the backup as of now"). Deleting them is the
   irreversible step and is not mine to take. Related: [[project_live_connections_and_demo]].
2. **Merge #1096** (#755) once CI is green — it was pending at session end. Then update
   `docs/progress.md` (Snapshot re-count + ledger row) per the post-merge hook.

## Shipped this session

| PR | Closes | Note |
|---|---|---|
| #1088 | — | IaC CLI Terraform → **OpenTofu**, both stacks (ADR 0024 amended in place; ADR 0021 too) |
| #1089 | — | Lineage env reconcile — **applied to prod** |
| #1092 | #1085 | Doc anchor + the out-of-band env-var rule |
| #1093 | #1087 | **State encryption** (AES-GCM + PBKDF2) — makes the OpenTofu swap *structural* |
| #1094 | #1072 | P1 — blank bool broke the documented fresh install |
| #1095 | #1067 | P1 — role-less Snowflake tested green, failed every run |
| #1096 | #755 | P1 — worker-lost run closure. **IN FLIGHT** |

## Pending — scoped with the user, not started

Order agreed: **#1091 next**, then reassess.

- **Batch 2 — #1091 + #1090 + #1052.** All three are "the product reports healthy while
  something is silently dead". Two PRs: (a) the **scheduling bug**, (b) a **staleness
  signal** independent of error/degraded, serving all three.
- **Batch 3 — #919 + #925.** Causally linked: #919 widens the asset population and #925's
  200-row browse cap *then* binds. Shipping #919 alone makes #925 worse. #919 still wants
  its own design pass.
- **Batch 4 — #892 + #912.** Warehouse-lineage graph quality; same code and tests.

### #1091 root cause is near-confirmed

Every daily task uses an **interval** (`"schedule": 86400.0`) and beat runs **embedded**
(`celery worker -B`) in an ephemeral container, so each worker restart resets the
countdown. **The comment in `celery_app.py` claims "prod uses a separate beat process";
`deploy/terraform/azure/containerapps.tf` shows `worker -B`. The comment is wrong about
prod.** Fix direction: crontab schedules (wall-clock, survive restarts) or persisted beat
state.

Live evidence: `snowflake` + `unity_catalog` lineage edges last refreshed **2026-07-18**,
and the two UC connections have **no error, no degraded reason, and no refresh** — only
consistent with the task never running. Six tasks share that schedule, including
`refresh_credential_expiry`, whose whole job is warning *before* a credential dies.

Also found: prod holds **zero `source='marquez'` edges** — the catalog pull was configured
but its target was `Stopped`, so #1090's purge is moot for this deployment; the code
defect is not.

## Gotchas that will recur

- **`-input=false` on every `tofu` invocation.** A missing required variable prompts on
  stdin; with stdout redirected the prompt is invisible and it **hangs forever**. Cost ~5h;
  root cause was a dropped `TF_VAR_app_db_password`, not the Azure throttling I first assumed.
- **State is encrypted — it cannot be grepped.** Use `tofu show -json`.
- **`pre-commit` does NOT cover `backend/tests/`** — CI runs `mypy backend/tests/`
  separately (#418). #1094 failed CI on exactly this.
- **`terraform.tfvars` outranks `TF_VAR_`** — a "wrong value" test via env var silently
  does nothing; use `-var`.
- **`model_construct` bypasses field aliases** (`schema=` leaves `schema_` unset).
- **Prod DB access**: temp single-IP Postgres firewall rule removed via a trap; the flag is
  `--name`, not `-r`.
- Direct `docs(progress):` / `docs(ops-log):` pushes to `main` are the established
  convention for post-merge bookkeeping (`d4123549`, `06a71d44`); everything else PRs.

## The lesson this session kept re-teaching

**Verify the reason, not just the result** — [[feedback_verify_the_reason_not_just_the_result]].

- I described the prod drift from the **rendered** plan; azurerm diffs `env` *positionally*,
  which hid the content and made me state the direction backwards. Only the `show -json`
  set-difference is honest. The user caught it by asking "what are those 2 changes?".
- Two guard tests in #1094 asserted things the architecture **deliberately denies**.
- A #755 test **passed for the wrong reason**; mutation-checking found the task-name guard
  could be deleted with nothing failing. See [[feedback_test_failure_modes]].
- I over-claimed harness verification in the ops log (`-refresh=false` compares to stored
  state, not live Azure) and had to narrow it.

1f245f43e29bc4d19193a32dad2b6cda84c354dc fix(worker): close the run when its worker child is killed, instead of waiting an hour (#1096)
commit 1f245f43e29bc4d19193a32dad2b6cda84c354dc
Author: Arijit Roy <royarijit1995@gmail.com>
Date:   Mon Jul 27 23:03:07 2026 -0700

    fix(worker): close the run when its worker child is killed, instead of waiting an hour (#1096)
    
    Closes #755
    
    When the OOM killer SIGKILLs a prefork child mid-`run_suite`, NOTHING inside the
    task executes — not the except, not the finally — so the run row could only be
    closed by the stuck-run reaper, up to `stuck_run_threshold_minutes` (default 60)
    later, with a reason that could say only "did not complete in time". Celery
    already knows the child was lost, so the information was there; nothing consumed it.
    
    Three of #755's four asks (the fourth is #595's size probe):
diff --git a/backend/app/services/run_service.py b/backend/app/services/run_service.py
index 5c684cbf..ef70601e 100644
--- a/backend/app/services/run_service.py
+++ b/backend/app/services/run_service.py
@@ -981,3 +981,43 @@ def reap_stuck_runs(
         for run_id in started_ids:
             lineage_dispatch.emit_run_lineage_terminal(session, run_id=run_id)
     return stuck
+
+
+def fail_run_worker_lost(
+    session: Session, *, run_id: uuid.UUID, now: datetime | None = None
+) -> bool:
+    """Drive a single run to ``failed`` after its worker process died (#755).
+
+    Called from the **parent** worker process via Celery's ``task_failure`` signal.
+    That indirection is the whole point: when the OOM killer SIGKILLs a prefork
+    child mid-``run_suite``, no code inside the task runs — not the ``except``, not
+    the ``finally`` — so the run row can only be closed by something that outlived
+    the child.
+
+    Without this the run sits ``running`` until :func:`reap_stuck_runs` catches it
+    ``stuck_run_threshold_minutes`` later (default **60**), with a reason that says
+    only "did not complete in time". Here Celery has already told us the child was
+    lost, so the failure is immediate and the reason names memory as the likely
+    cause instead of leaving the user to guess.
+
+    Idempotent and non-clobbering: a run that already reached a terminal status is
+    left alone and ``False`` is returned. This matters because the signal can fire
+    for a task whose run was cancelled, or which finished and died afterwards —
+    neither should be rewritten to ``failed``.
+    """
+    run = session.get(Run, run_id)
+    if run is None or run.status not in _NON_TERMINAL_STATUSES:
+        return False
+    moment = now or _now()
+    was_running = run.status == "running"
+    run_dispatch.mark_dispatch_failed(run, at=moment, reason=run_dispatch.WORKER_LOST_REASON)
+    session.commit()
+    log.warning("run_failed_worker_lost", run_id=str(run_id), was_running=was_running)
+    # Same contract as the reaper: a `running` run emitted an OpenLineage START that
+    # would otherwise dangle forever; a `queued` one never did. Lazy import breaks
+    # the lineage<->run_service cycle; fail-open and dark by default.
+    if was_running:
+        from backend.app.lineage import dispatch as lineage_dispatch
+
+        lineage_dispatch.emit_run_lineage_terminal(session, run_id=run_id)
+    return True

| ✅ | [#1095](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1095) **Snowflake `role` required on every connection** (`Closes #1067`) — GX's `REQUIRED_QUERY_PARAMS` is `{warehouse, role}`, so a role-less connection produced a DSN GX rejects at `add_snowflake`. The validator already encoded this reasoning but scoped it to key-pair: **the reasoning was right, the scope was wrong** — the requirement is GX's, not the auth method's. One line, plus the part that matters: **two mutation-checked guard tests**, because nothing checked the shipped template was loadable. Writing them was the lesson — **two attempts asserted things the architecture deliberately denies** (`.env.example` isn't a Settings file, `extra=forbid`/#209; the RAW template isn't meant to load because secret keys ship blank by design). The assertion is *"the .env.app setup.sh produces must load"*; both exclusions are documented so nobody re-tightens them | config / P1 |

| ✅ | [#1093](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1093) **OpenTofu state encryption** (`Closes #1087`) — AES-GCM + PBKDF2 over state **and** plan files; state held the generated Postgres password, the Redis password and webhook secrets as plaintext on one laptop. **The obvious key store was a trap**: Key Vault is managed BY the state it would encrypt and purge-protection is off, so lose-vault ⇒ lose-key ⇒ unreadable state ⇒ cannot rebuild the vault. Key lives in the gitignored `terraform.tfvars` — **not `.env`**, which `scripts/setup.sh` regenerates, and regenerating it would make the state permanently unreadable. **Claim kept honest**: the key sits beside the ciphertext, so it buys little against host compromise and a lot against *accidental* disclosure (committed state, a `.tfstate.backup` swept into a backup, a state pasted into a ticket). **Rehearsed on a throwaway stack before touching prod**, which settled four assumptions — incl. that a **no-op apply still rewrites state** (decisive, our plan is clean) — and one rehearsal check was *invalid on first run* because `terraform.tfvars` outranks `TF_VAR_`, so the "wrong passphrase" never reached the block. Verified on the real stack: plan `exitcode=0`, wrong passphrase `exit 1 / cipher: message authentication failed`, re-plan `0` (uncorrupted). **This makes the ADR 0024 OpenTofu swap STRUCTURAL** — Terraform cannot parse `encryption {}`. Two operational consequences documented: the state can no longer be grepped (`tofu show -json`), and **`-input=false` is mandatory** — a missing required var prompts on stdin and, with stdout redirected, hangs invisibly (**cost ~5h this session**; root cause was a dropped `TF_VAR_app_db_password`, *not* the Azure throttling I first assumed). Plaintext backups deliberately **retained** pending an off-machine copy of the passphrase | security / IaC |

Consecutive, not a rate — a Redis dropping one request in five is annoying, not degraded, and opening for it would silently switch enforcement off across the whole API. **The review found two things worth the ink.** (1) A straggling success could close an open breaker: every request is an independent asyncio task over shared module globals, so one that passed the gate just BEFORE the trip and resolved just after would retroactively close a breaker others had legitimately opened — and a degraded Redis serves exactly that mix of slow successes and timeouts, so it would flap under precisely the traffic it exists to handle. content.text:
Provide a code review for the given pull request.

To do this, follow these steps precisely:

1. Use a Haiku agent to check if the pull request (a) is closed, (b) is a draft, (c) does not need a code review (eg. because it is an automated pull request, or is very simple and obviously ok), or (d) already has a code review from you from earlier. If so, do not proceed.
2. Use another Haiku agent to give you a list of file paths to (but not the contents of) any relevant CLAUDE.md files from the codebase: the root CLAUDE.md file (if one exists), as well as any CLAUDE.md files in the directories whose files the pull request modified
3. Use a Haiku agent to view the pull request, and ask the agent to return a summary of the change
4. Then, launch 5 parallel Sonnet agents to independently code review the change. The agents should do the following, then return a list of issues and the reason each issue was flagged (eg. CLAUDE.md adherence, bug, historical git context, etc.):
   a. Agent #1: Audit the changes to make sure they compily with the CLAUDE.md. Note that CLAUDE.md is guidance for Claude as it writes code, so not all instructions will be applicable during code review.
   b. Agent #2: Read the file changes in the pull request, then do a shallow scan for obvious bugs. Avoid reading extra context beyond the changes, focusing just on the changes themselves. Focus on large bugs, and avoid small issues and nitpicks. Ignore likely false positives.
   c. Agent #3: Read the git blame and history of the code modified, to identify any bugs in light of that historical context
   d. Agent #4: Read previous pull requests that touched these files, and check for any comments on those pull requests that may also apply to the current pull request.
   e. Agent #5: Read code comments in the modified files, and make sure the changes in the pull request comply with any guidance in the comments.
5. For each issue found in #4, launch a parallel Haiku agent that takes the PR, issue description, and list of CLAUDE.md files (from step 2), and returns a score to indicate the agent's level of confidence for whether the issue is real or false positive. To do that, the agent should score each issue on a scale from 0-100, indicating its level of confidence. For issues that were flagged due to CLAUDE.md instructions, the agent should double check that the CLAUDE.md actually calls out that issue specifically. The scale is (give this rubric to the agent verbatim):
   a. 0: Not confident at all. This is a false positive that doesn't stand up to light scrutiny, or is a pre-existing issue.
   b. 25: Somewhat confident. This might be a real issue, but may also be a false positive. The agent wasn't able to verify that it's a real issue. If the issue is stylistic, it is one that was not explicitly called out in the relevant CLAUDE.md.
   c. 50: Moderately confident. The agent was able to verify this is a real issue, but it might be a nitpick or not happen very often in practice. Relative to the rest of the PR, it's not very important.
   d. 75: Highly confident. The agent double checked the issue, and verified that it is very likely it is a real issue that will be hit in practice. The existing approach in the PR is insufficient. The issue is very important and will directly impact the code's functionality, or it is an issue that is directly mentioned in the relevant CLAUDE.md.
   e. 100: Absolutely certain. The agent double checked the issue, and confirmed that it is definitely a real issue, that will happen frequently in practice. The evidence directly confirms this.
6. Filter out any issues with a score less than 80. If there are no issues that meet this criteria, do not proceed.
7. Use a Haiku agent to repeat the eligibility check from #1, to make sure that the pull request is still eligible for code review.
8. Finally, use the gh bash command to comment back on the pull request with the result. When writing your comment, keep in mind to:
   a. Keep your output brief
   b. Avoid emojis
   c. Link and cite relevant code, files, and URLs

Examples of false positives, for steps 4 and 5:

- Pre-existing issues
- Something that looks like a bug but is not actually a bug
- Pedantic nitpicks that a senior engineer wouldn't call out
- Issues that a linter, typechecker, or compiler would catch (eg. missing or incorrect imports, type errors, broken tests, formatting issues, pedantic style issues like newlines). No need to run these build steps yourself -- it is safe to assume that they will be run separately as part of CI.
- General code quality issues (eg. lack of test coverage, general security issues, poor documentation), unless explicitly required in CLAUDE.md
- Issues that are called out in CLAUDE.md, but explicitly silenced in the code (eg. due to a lint ignore comment)
- Changes in functionality that are likely intentional or are directly related to the broader change
- Real issues, but on lines that the user did not modify in their pull request

Notes:

- Do not check build signal or attempt to build or typecheck the app. These will run separately, and are not relevant to your code review.
- Use `gh` to interact with Github (eg. to fetch a pull request, or to create inline comments), rather than web fetch
- Make a todo list first
- You must cite and link each bug (eg. if referring to a CLAUDE.md, you must link it)
- For your final comment, follow the following format precisely (assuming for this example that you found 3 issues):

---

### Code review

Found 3 issues:

1. <brief description of bug> (CLAUDE.md says "<...>")

<link to file and line with full sha1 + line range for context, note that you MUST provide the full sha and not use bash here, eg. https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/1d54823877c4de72b2316a64032a54afc404e619/README.md#L13-L17>

2. <brief description of bug> (some/other/CLAUDE.md says "<...>")

<link to file and line with full sha1 + line range for context>

3. <brief description of bug> (bug due to <file and code snippet>)

<link to file and line with full sha1 + line range for context>

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)

<sub>- If this code review was useful, please react with 👍. Otherwise, react with 👎.</sub>

---

- Or, if you found no issues:

---

### Code review

No issues found. Checked for bugs and CLAUDE.md compliance.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)

- When linking to code, follow the following format precisely, otherwise the Markdown preview won't render correctly: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-cli-internal/blob/c21d3c10bc8e898b7ac1a2d745bdc9bc4e423afe/package.json#L10-L15
  - Requires full git sha
  - You must provide the full sha. Commands like `https://github.com/owner/repo/blob/$(git rev-parse HEAD)/foo/bar` will not work, since your comment will be directly rendered in Markdown.
  - Repo name must match the repo you're code reviewing
  - # sign after the file name
  - Line range format is L[start]-L[end]
  - Provide at least 1 line of context before and after, centered on the line you are commenting about (eg. if you are commenting about lines 5-6, you should link to `L4-7`)

The case that actually happens is the FIRST `/me` being throttled, where there is no cached answer to hold and the fix is to stay loading and retry — a different shape from the issue's sketch. **Writing the test is what exposed it**, which is the session's recurring lesson arriving from the other direction: not a test that proves nothing, but a test that refuses to be written because the behaviour isn't there.) (**2026-07-26 (later) — LIVE TESTING against the fresh prod deploy found a real defect that three green suites could not.** A non-interactive bearer (`az account get-access-token` on the api scope, #565) against `/api/v1/connections` showed **both Airflow connections at 282 and 280 consecutive poll failures** — ~47 hours broken. **That diagnosis was WRONG and is corrected on the issue** — I read the 404 and the `/api/v1/` URL shape and concluded Airflow 3 had moved the API to `/api/v2/`, without checking whether the host was up. It is not: `dataq-harness-airflow` is **`Stopped`**, deliberately, per the 2026-07-04 cost wind-down (#590), and ACA's ingress serves its unavailable page with a 404. `/api/v2/version` returns the same Azure error page, which would have said so immediately. [#1023](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1023) is rescoped to what survives: the classified reason tells the operator to check a connection config that is fine, when the signal is really that the host is unreachable — and a deliberately-offline integration now accumulates unbounded failures AND alerts (#842/#843), which wants a decision rather than a default. **The lesson is the one already written down and not applied: verify the reason, not just the result** — a green-looking inference from a status code is still an inference. Two things worth keeping: **#828's health counter is what made it findable at all** — that fact used to live only in logs — and **the classified reason points the wrong way**, telling the operator to 'check the connection and the suite's run target' when nothing is wrong with either; a 404 from a KNOWN provider endpoint is a version-compatibility signal, not a user misconfiguration. Also filed [#1024](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1024): `credential_expires_at` is NULL on all 13 prod connections including the two SAS-bearing ADLS ones, because #838 computes on secret write plus a DAILY sweep — so on a fresh deploy the feature delivers nothing for the existing estate for up to 24h, and NULL now means both 'no readable expiry' and 'not looked yet', which the UI cannot distinguish. **Neither would have surfaced from any test: one needed a live provider at its real version, the other needed a deploy with pre-existing rows.**) (**2026-07-26 (later still) — #788 CLOSED**, the last AC landing in the shape that actually occurs rather than the one sketched. The per-IP unauth bucket is shared across endpoints, so a burst anywhere can 429 `/me` — and painting PageError for it is wrong twice over: the app is fine, and the answer arrives on its own seconds later, meanwhile a workspace admin has lost the Admin and Settings nav. `MeProvider` now stays in `loading` and retries when the server said to; a spinner is the honest state where an error page asserts something false. Bounded at three retries, because **an endless spinner is the one outcome worse than an error page** — indistinguishable from a hung app, with nothing to act on. Non-429 failures are untouched (a 500/403 is not self-healing and must reach PageError with its HTTP facts, #910/#930). The mutation check earned its keep twice: it confirmed all three retry tests are load-bearing, AND it exposed a leak in those tests — `vi.useRealTimers()` sat at the end of each test BODY, which a failing test never reaches, so fake timers bled into the next test and it timed out for a reason unrelated to its assertion. Three real failures plus one phantom; moved to `afterEach`. **Batch 5 now stands at #976 and #788 done, #936 and #925 open.**) (**2026-07-26 (end of day) — ops log + hook, and HARNESS_TODO retired.** Two incidents this week shared one shape: state that mattered lived only outside git, so nobody could tell a deliberate action from a fault. New [docs/ops-log.md](ops-log.md) records harness start/stop and credential rotation — the latter listing EVERY Key Vault secret written per rotation, the countermeasure to the partial rotation that left two Snowflake connections dead for three weeks. Git-tracked deliberately rather than harness-side: history is the point, and an untracked file has none. A `PostToolUse:Bash` hook keeps it current; **it took three attempts and every failure was the same mistake** — it fired on its own commit message (grepped the whole string), then still fired after anchoring (prose WORD-WRAPS, so a line began `harness_window.sh.`), and finally needed a whitespace-or-end boundary, because a real invocation is followed by arguments or nothing, never a full stop. Then I chased a fourth phantom before testing the real hook against the real command and finding it silent. **Three variations of reasoning about what a pattern would match instead of running it** — the same root as the Airflow misdiagnosis that morning. **`HARNESS_TODO.md` removed**, but only after reading it: it held TWO open items, not the one already filed. The second — the deployed Terraform still injects `SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD` into the Airflow ACA env and dbt job, dead under the 2026-07-18 MFA enforcement — **would have been destroyed with the file**, and is invisible today only because the harness is stopped. Now [#1030](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1030) and [#1032](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1032), original archived verbatim in #1032. It also supplied the *why* Azure never could: the harness was stopped ~15 min after that MFA wall. **Rule now recorded: anything still open belongs in the tracker; only settled notes belong harness-side.**) (**2026-07-26 (close) — #1024 cold-start half fixed.** `refresh_credential_expiry` ran DAILY, which is right for a value that only moves on a rotation and wrong for a cold start: a freshly deployed instance showed `credential_expires_at` NULL until the first tick, and **NULL renders as 'nothing expires soon' — indistinguishable from 'we have not looked yet'**, so the warning surface read as reassuring for up to 24h. Prod had exactly that after this morning's deploy, including the SAS-bearing connections whose expiry is printed in the token. Now dispatched from `beat_init` beside the existing gap recovery (one beat process per deployment → once per restart, not once per worker). The two startup tasks became a list with **independently guarded** dispatch — a single `try` around the loop would let the first broker hiccup silently drop every later task, and that failure looks identical to success because dispatch is fire-and-forget. Mutation-verified both ways. **#1024 stays OPEN for its second half**: NULL still conflates 'no readable expiry' (a Snowflake PAT — correctly unknowable) with 'not computed yet'; this shrinks the ambiguity window from a day to seconds without removing it.) (**2026-07-26 — TIER 1 (security) DONE: #989 closed.** A monitor's error message interpolated the offending target CELL, and that message is safe-marked — persisted verbatim into `results.observed_value` and rendered in the UI, alerts and MCP, none of which consult the suite's column policy. A freshness monitor aimed at a declared-PII column echoed its value straight past the redaction machinery built for exactly that. It also made the marker's own rule false, which is how a rule erodes. **Built at the READ layer, not by threading a policy into `datasources/`** — my first scoping said the latter; reading `redact_sample_failures` showed the product already stores samples raw and masks at the read boundaries, so threading a policy down would have inverted that dependency to fix a redaction bug. Message is now value-free by construction; the cell rides `MonitorConfigError.unparsed_value` and is masked by the new `redact_observed_value` under the same authority as the sample path (shown unless *known* sensitive — default-masking would make 'your timestamp column has junk in it' unactionable, the reason option (a) was rejected). **The review earned its keep: it found a FOURTH sink I had missed** — `/_probe/runs/{run_id}` mapped Result rows straight through Pydantic, so a cell masked everywhere else surfaced raw there. Fixed with a test. That is the failure mode of per-sink redaction, and why each sink needs its own test rather than one test for 'the redactor'. It also surfaced something worse, filed as [#1039](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1039): that route has **no suite-ownership check at all**, so any authenticated user with a run UUID reads any run's results, bypassing ADR 0027 — and it is mounted in prod. Two bugs on one forgotten Week-1 route in a single PR is an argument for deleting it.) (**2026-07-26 — TIER 2 (connection health) DONE: #998, #1024, #748, #999, #996.** Sequenced by dependency, and the order mattered every time. **#998** replaced the connection-wide failure count with per-suite streaks rolled up — a broken hourly suite used to fill the shared 20-run window and badge a connection whose credential was fine, telling the operator to re-auth something that worked; a connection is now degraded only when EVERY suite is failing, with the MINIMUM streak as the number (the strongest claim true of all of them). **#1024** gave NULL expiry one meaning via `credential_expiry_checked_at` — stamped on every read, so 'no readable expiry' stops being indistinguishable from 'never looked', which is what made an unchecked credential look safe. **#748** added `/readyz` (a real DB read, 2s-bounded) because during the 2026-07-10 lock incident `/healthz` stayed GREEN through 25 minutes of total read degradation; `/healthz` stays liveness-only on purpose, since a liveness probe that fails on a DB blip gets the container killed. **#999** is the one where measuring changed the answer: the planned index ALONE only halves a cost that stays linear in history (8.4→32.7→195.4ms at 1k/4k/16k runs per suite; with index 5.5→23.0→94.8ms). LATERAL alone is also linear. Only **both** are flat — **0.2ms at every size** — because the index lets Postgres stop after 20 entries per suite. AC 3 said 'measured, not assumed' and it was right to. **#996** then fired the alert edges off the run streak, reusing #843's delivery-driven logic rather than a second copy. **Three guards caught things I would have shipped:** two alembic revision-id COLLISIONS (I verified the id for one migration then hand-picked the next), the #990 model-vs-migration parity test catching the new index undeclared, and the #787 assert-side-effect guard catching my own test. **And a mutation survived that mattered** — deleting #996's hook from `run_suite` broke nothing, so the alerting could have shipped connected to nothing. Third instance this session of a safeguard that looks wired up and isn't, after the dead mock in #976 and the unwired redaction sink in #989.) (**2026-07-26 (night) — TIER 3 under way: #1039, #727, #905.** **#1039** deleted the unauthorized probe run reader — `GET /_probe/runs/{id}` read any run's results for ANY authenticated user, no suite-ownership check, mounted in prod; a UUID is not a capability token. Deleted rather than gated, because being a forgotten sibling is precisely how it escaped #989's redaction sweep two PRs earlier, and pinned as a 404 so it cannot creep back. **#727** moved target-shape resolution into `datasources/registry.py`, ending a second dispatch-by-type site that silently falsified the 'adding a datasource is one registry entry' contract (#716 already had to edit both) — now enforced by a test comparing the adapter set against the resolver set, not by a comment asking people to remember. **#905 closed by triage, not by building:** item 1 (beat liveness) shipped in #904 and was verified live today; item 2's stated goal — a wedged reconnect dies rather than hanging — is **met by item 1**, cause-agnostically, which is the property the issue itself argued for. I deliberately did NOT pin broker settings on top: the issue asks to *investigate* why the reconnect loop neither retried nor raised, I cannot establish that without reproducing the wedge, and shipping unverified settings against live prod is a placebo. Item 3 became [#1052](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1052) — workspace-wide `last_polled_at` staleness, the one signal that cannot lie, because every incident in this class is the worker looking alive and writing nothing, so anything derived from its own writes cannot fire when it is what broke. **Harness credentials fixed for #1032:** ACCOUNTADMIN PAT → the terraform provider (it creates account roles; `DATAQ_LOADER` cannot create itself), loader PAT → the KV secret the containers read; both verified by asserting `CURRENT_ROLE()`, not by the write succeeding. The targeted apply propagated it — **5 of the plan's 8 changes**, because a blanket apply would have ARMED both ADF triggers (`activated false -> true`) on a harness meant to be asleep, and silently altered the warehouse via provider drift. All five harness apps verified `Stopped` afterwards.)

(**2026-07-25 (later) — standing rule added + a self-inflicted register bug found and fixed.** **CONTRIBUTING rule 3a / CLAUDE.md §11: "pre-existing" is not a disposition** (user, this session) — DataQ is in prod, so a defect's age says nothing about its blast radius; every finding ends **fixed or filed**, never noted-in-a-reply or buried in a docstring. Verified-benign is a valid outcome *if the determination is recorded*; unexamined is not. Discharged immediately against my own session: two findings I had documented in code but never filed are now [#989](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/989) (`SafeMonitorError` echoes a target cell value, which its own rule forbids — bounded and arguably justified, but the redaction policy has no say in it) and [#990](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/990) (**model-vs-migration schema parity is never checked anywhere** — the test schema is `create_all`, so #457's guard covers 2 of the 3 predicate spellings, and this same gap is what let #913's mistargeted backfill migration break every fresh database). **The register bug: three PRs claimed 13 issues and closed 3.** GitHub honours only the **first** issue after a `Closes` keyword; the rest of a comma list are ignored **silently**. Ten issues sat open against shipped work — and this repo already recorded the same trap on the #720 batch, which is exactly why knowing it is not enough. All ten closed by hand with their merging PR named; the countermeasure is now structural rather than memorial — the **PR template** carries the one-keyword-per-issue rule *and* the post-merge `gh issue view` verification loop.) (**2026-07-25 — verification sweep + three closing PRs: 89 → 82 open, 15 issues resolved.** Six agents re-checked 48 candidate issues **against the tree, not the ticket** — the discipline that caught #724 the day before. **Closed on evidence, no code needed (6):** #322/#573 (both already fixed, tracked to completion under later duplicates #640/#714 — verified in-tree and re-run), #929 (subset of #787, which now carries a fresh count: **112** sites across 14 files, not the filing-time ~93), #893 (warehouse lineage WAS live-verified on both warehouses in the 07-18 arc; evidence quoted onto the issue), #731 (findings register discharged — 3 of 5 children closed, 2 tracked), #541 (**the audit is the deliverable**: both 500-risk paths are closed — `pipeline_runs` cascades, `suites.connection_id` 409s at the service layer — and the three remaining `users.id` FKs are latent by design, with the revisit trigger recorded on the issue). **Shipped (9):** [#984](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/984) docs/SAST (#729/#730/#800/#806), [#985](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/985) frontend (#915/#916/#949/#563/#601), [#986](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/986) backend (#900/#306/#728/#457). **The reviews were again worth more than the features.** #984's first attempt **broke the SAST gate**: I removed five bandit suppressions after counting *warnings* (37 → 0) instead of the gate's **exit code**, which went 0 → 5 findings. The diagnosis was wrong too — each site had TWO markers, one on the flagged node (load-bearing) and one outside its range (inert), and the `no failed test` warning names the inert one without saying which is which. All five restored, bare; the prose-tokenization half was real and stays fixed (20 warnings gone); the residual 17 are **intrinsic** to a marker on a multi-line node, so #806's "zero warnings" AC was a false premise and is recorded as such. #900's obvious fix (classify everything) was likewise wrong and **six existing tests said so** — it turned "unknown freshness column 'nope'" into "the run failed to execute", so safety is now *declared* via a `SafeMonitorError` marker rather than guessed. Reviewers also caught two places where my own text overclaimed: the #915 comment asserted `last_error`/`degraded_reason` were exclusive (they are not → [#987](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/987)), and the #457 guard's docstring claimed three coverages while checking two (the migration is never applied in the test schema) — both corrected to state the hole rather than imply it is closed. **Two lessons banked:** *judge a suppression by the gate's exit code, never its warning count* (now CONTRIBUTING rule 16), and *a subagent's `git checkout` moves YOUR HEAD* — a background review agent stranded a commit on local `main` mid-session; recovered via reflog + `cherry-pick --no-commit`, and reviewers are now told to stay read-only.) New [docs/ops-log.md](ops-log.md) records harness start/stop and credential rotation — the latter listing EVERY Key Vault secret written per rotation, the countermeasure to the partial rotation that left two Snowflake connections dead for three weeks. Git-tracked deliberately rather than harness-side: history is the point, and an untracked file has none. A `PostToolUse:Bash` hook keeps it current; **it took three attempts and every failure was the same mistake** — it fired on its own commit message (grepped the whole string), then still fired after anchoring (prose WORD-WRAPS, so a line began `harness_window.sh.`), and finally needed a whitespace-or-end boundary, because a real invocation is followed by arguments or nothing, never a full stop. Prod had exactly that after this morning's deploy, including the SAS-bearing connections whose expiry is printed in the token. Now dispatched from `beat_init` beside the existing gap recovery (one beat process per deployment → once per restart, not once per worker). The two startup tasks became a list with **independently guarded** dispatch — a single `try` around the loop would let the first broker hiccup silently drop every later task, and that failure looks identical to success because dispatch is fire-and-forget. Mutation-verified both ways. **#1024 stays OPEN for its second half**: NULL still conflates 'no readable expiry' (a Snowflake PAT — correctly unknowable) with 'not computed yet'; this shrinks the ambiguity window from a day to seconds without removing it.) (**2026-07-26 — TIER 1 (security) DONE: #989 closed.** A monitor's error message interpolated the offending target CELL, and that message is safe-marked — persisted verbatim into `results.observed_value` and rendered in the UI, alerts and MCP, none of which consult the suite's column policy. A freshness monitor aimed at a declared-PII column echoed its value straight past the redaction machinery built for exactly that. It also made the marker's own rule false, which is how a rule erodes. **Built at the READ layer, not by threading a policy into `datasources/`** — my first scoping said the latter; reading `redact_sample_failures` showed the product already stores samples raw and masks at the read boundaries, so threading a policy down would have inverted that dependency to fix a redaction bug. Message is now value-free by construction; the cell rides `MonitorConfigError.unparsed_value` and is masked by the new `redact_observed_value` under the same authority as the sample path (shown unless *known* sensitive — default-masking would make 'your timestamp column has junk in it' unactionable, the reason option (a) was rejected). **The review earned its keep: it found a FOURTH sink I had missed** — `/_probe/runs/{run_id}` mapped Result rows straight through Pydantic, so a cell masked everywhere else surfaced raw there. Fixed with a test. That is the failure mode of per-sink redaction, and why each sink needs its own test rather than one test for 'the redactor'. It also surfaced something worse, filed as [#1039](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1039): that route has **no suite-ownership check at all**, so any authenticated user with a run UUID reads any run's results, bypassing ADR 0027 — and it is mounted in prod. LATERAL alone is also linear. Only **both** are flat — **0.2ms at every size** — because the index lets Postgres stop after 20 entries per suite. AC 3 said 'measured, not assumed' and it was right to. **#996** then fired the alert edges off the run streak, reusing #843's delivery-driven logic rather than a second copy. **Three guards caught things I would have shipped:** two alembic revision-id COLLISIONS (I verified the id for one migration then hand-picked the next), the #990 model-vs-migration parity test catching the new index undeclared, and the #787 assert-side-effect guard catching my own test. **And a mutation survived that mattered** — deleting #996's hook from `run_suite` broke nothing, so the alerting could have shipped connected to nothing. Third instance this session of a safeguard that looks wired up and isn't, after the dead mock in #976 and the unwired redaction sink in #989.) I deliberately did NOT pin broker settings on top: the issue asks to *investigate* why the reconnect loop neither retried nor raised, I cannot establish that without reproducing the wedge, and shipping unverified settings against live prod is a placebo. countdown. **The comment in `celery_app.py` claims "prod uses a separate beat process";

prod.** Fix direction: crontab schedules (wall-clock, survive restarts) or persisted beat

content.content:
# beat: daily tasks appear not to have run since 2026-07-18 — warehouse lineage silently 9 days stale, and staleness is invisible

Found while resolving #1090 against **live prod**, immediately after the #1089 apply.

## Evidence

```
lineage_edges by source          -- source='marquez' returns ZERO rows
 dbt           |  8 | last_seen 2026-07-27 06:56   <- current
 snowflake     |  8 | last_seen 2026-07-18 19:16   <- 9 days stale
 unity_catalog | 12 | last_seen 2026-07-18 19:16   <- 9 days stale

connections (warehouse lineage state)
 unity_catalog | 2 conns | ever_refreshed 2 | most_recent 2026-07-18 19:16 | errors 0 | degraded 0
 snowflake     | 3 conns | ever_refreshed 3 | most_recent 2026-07-18 19:16 | errors 2 | degraded 1
```

`WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_ENABLED=true` has been live on the worker throughout, and
`refresh_warehouse_lineage` is scheduled every 86400s.

## The inference

The two **Unity Catalog** connections are the tell. They have **zero errors and zero
degraded reasons**, yet have not refreshed since 2026-07-18. If the task had run:
- and UC succeeded → `lineage_last_refresh_at` would be recent;
- and UC failed → an error would be recorded (the task is fail-soft *per connection* and
  "records a classified error").

Neither is true, so **the task has not executed since 2026-07-18**. (The 2 Snowflake
errors are separately explained by the dead PATs in #954 — that is not this.)

## Suspected cause — interval schedules + ephemeral embedded beat

Every daily task uses an **interval**, not a crontab:

```python
"schedule": 86400.0,  # 24 hours
```

...and beat runs **embedded** in the worker (`celery ... worker -B`) in a Container App
with no persistent beat state. An interval schedule restarts its countdown when beat
restarts, so **if the worker restarts more often than every 24h, a daily task never
fires.** ACA rolls revisions, scales, and the #904 watchdog deliberately restarts a wedged
worker — all of which reset the timer.

Six tasks are on this schedule and would all be affected:
`purge_sample_failures`, `sweep_orphan_assets`, `sweep_orphan_secrets`,
`refresh_lineage_pull`, `refresh_warehouse_lineage`, `refresh_credential_expiry`.

That last one is notable: **credential-expiry warnings (#838) exist precisely to warn
before a credential dies** — and #954 records two PATs that died without warning.

## The second defect — staleness has no signal

`failing_lineage_sources` ([`asset_view_service.py:626-632`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/backend/app/services/asset_view_service.py#L626-L632)) requires
`lineage_last_refresh_at IS NOT NULL` **AND** (`degraded_reason` OR `last_error`). A source
that simply **stops being refreshed** — no error, no degradation — matches nothing, so the
2 UC connections render as healthy while serving 9-day-old lineage.

This is the #828 / #954 / #953 shape again: the product reports a healthy state for
something that is not doing its job.

## AC

- Confirm the cause (check beat logs / whether any 86400s task has fired since a restart).
- If confirmed, move daily tasks to **crontab** schedules (fire at a wall-clock time,
  survive restarts) rather than intervals — or persist beat state.
- Add a **staleness** signal: a lineage source whose last refresh is older than ~2x its
  cadence should surface, independently of error/degraded.
- Re-verify `refresh_credential_expiry` actually runs, given #838's purpose.

## Related

#1090, #1086, #954 (dead PATs), #904 (beat watchdog), #838 (credential expiry), #828, ADR 0034.

with no persistent beat state. An interval schedule restarts its countdown when beat
restarts, so **if the worker restarts more often than every 24h, a daily task never
fires.** ACA rolls revisions, scales, and the #904 watchdog deliberately restarts a wedged
worker — all of which reset the timer.

Six tasks are on this schedule and would all be affected:
`purge_sample_failures`, `sweep_orphan_assets`, `sweep_orphan_secrets`,
`refresh_lineage_pull`, `refresh_warehouse_lineage`, `refresh_credential_expiry`.

That last one is notable: **credential-expiry warnings (#838) exist precisely to warn
before a credential dies** — and #954 records two PATs that died without warning.

## The second defect — staleness has no signal

`failing_lineage_sources` ([`asset_view_service.py:626-632`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/backend/app/services/asset_view_service.py#L626-L632)) requires
`lineage_last_refresh_at IS NOT NULL` **AND** (`degraded_reason` OR `last_error`). A source
that simply **stops being refreshed** — no error, no degradation — matches nothing, so the
2 UC connections render as healthy while serving 9-day-old lineage.

This is the #828 / #954 / #953 shape again: the product reports a healthy state for
something that is not doing its job.

## AC

- Confirm the cause (check beat logs / whether any 86400s task has fired since a restart).
- If confirmed, move daily tasks to **crontab** schedules (fire at a wall-clock time,
  survive restarts) rather than intervals — or persist beat state.
- Add a **staleness** signal: a lineage source whose last refresh is older than ~2x its
  cadence should surface, independently of error/degraded.
- Re-verify `refresh_credential_expiry` actually runs, given #838's purpose.

## Related

#1090, #1086, #954 (dead PATs), #904 (beat watchdog), #838 (credential expiry), #828, ADR 0034.

# lineage: removing LINEAGE_PROVIDER freezes cached marquez edges forever, with no health signal

Surfaced by review of #1089, which will remove `LINEAGE_PROVIDER` / `MARQUEZ_URL` from prod.

## What

Once `LINEAGE_PROVIDER` is unset, any `lineage_edges` rows with `source='marquez'` are
**never refreshed and never pruned again** — and nothing tells anyone.

Verified in code:

- `refresh_lineage_pull` ([`backend/app/worker/tasks.py:995-997`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/backend/app/worker/tasks.py#L995-L997)) calls `get_lineage_provider()`, which returns `None` the moment `lineage_provider` is empty ([`backend/app/lineage/pull.py:72-74`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/backend/app/lineage/pull.py#L72-L74)), and the task then `return 0` **before opening a session**.
- `_prune_stale` is only reachable from inside `refresh_pulled_edges` (`pull.py:166`, `:198`). Short-circuiting above it means stale rows are never swept.
- `failing_lineage_sources` ([`asset_view_service.py:650`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/backend/app/services/asset_view_service.py#L650)) is **scoped to `dbt`** by its own docstring — the Marquez pull has no backing `Connection` row, so it can never appear there.

Net: the edges sit in the asset graph **looking exactly like current data**, with no badge, no caveat, and no way for a user to learn the source was switched off.

## Why it matters

This is the #828 / #954 shape again — a thing the product renders as healthy while it
cannot do its job. Worse here than a failing poll, because a failing poll at least logs;
an unconfigured one is silent by design.

Note the fail-soft path is fine: a *reachable-but-erroring* `MARQUEZ_URL` is caught and
skips pruning deliberately (cross-source safety). The gap is specifically **config removed
entirely**.

## AC

- Decide the disposition for orphaned pulled edges when a provider is de-configured:
  either sweep them (a `source` no longer configured ⇒ purge), or mark them stale and
  surface that in the asset view.
- If surfaced, the signal must not be `dbt`-scoped — widen the lineage-source health
  surface to cover the catalog pull, per its own docstring's "widening it means adding a
  provider, not rewriting this".
- Operationally: check whether prod currently holds `source='marquez'` rows and purge them
  as part of the #1086 apply if so.

## Related

#1086 (the reconciliation that triggers this), #1089, ADR 0034, #828, #954.
======
# alerting: workspace-wide last_polled_at staleness — the signal that cannot lie

Split out of #905 (item 3), which is closed for its other two items.

## Why this one is different from what we already have

#828/#954/#996 alert **per connection**, from state the worker itself writes. Every incident in the #905 class — #852 exporter starvation, #854 unbounded row-lock wait, the 2026-07-18 wedged broker reconnect — had the same shape: **the worker looks alive and writes nothing**. A per-connection signal derived from worker writes cannot fire when the worker is the thing that is broken.

The DB is the only party that can tell. If `max(last_polled_at)` across **all** orchestration connections is older than a few poll intervals, the polling loop is dead regardless of cause — no theory about which subsystem wedged, no dependence on the worker noticing its own silence.

That is the #852 lesson stated as a rule: *the DB was the only truth.*

## What #905 already covers, so this doesn't duplicate it

The beat watchdog (#904) restarts a worker whose heartbeat goes stale, which is the *self-healing* half. This is the *telling-a-human* half — and they fail independently. A watchdog that itself never runs (wrong image, disabled env, crash before arming) leaves nobody informed, and the 2026-07-18 outage was found manually after six hours.

## Direction

- A periodic check — cheap, one `SELECT max(last_polled_at)` over orchestration connections.
- Alert when it exceeds N × the poll interval, through the existing `HealthPublisher` seam.
- **Must not run in the same process whose liveness it reports on**, or it inherits the failure it exists to detect. Options: the API side (it serves requests and can run a background check), or an external probe hitting a new endpoint.
- Recovery edge on the same delivery-flag rule as #843/#996.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Workspace-wide poll staleness raises an alert without depending on the worker being healthy
- [ ] The check does not live solely in the process it monitors
- [ ] Reuses the `HealthPublisher` seam and the #843 delivered-first rule; no parallel mechanism
- [ ] A test where the worker writes nothing at all and the alert still fires

## Related

#905 (parent), #852, #854, #904 (the watchdog half), #843/#996 (the edge rules).

        # -> 1666 MiB across three runs). The child is replaced BETWEEN tasks, so
        # this never interrupts a run in flight; it only stops memory creep.
        # 0 disables.
        worker_max_memory_per_child=settings.worker_max_memory_per_child_kb or None,
        # Deliberately NOT acks_late. With early ack (the default) a task the broker
        # has already delivered is not redelivered when the child dies — which is
        # exactly what stops an OOM-killing run from being handed straight back to a
        # fresh child and killing it too (#755's poison-pill ask; a local crash loop
        # of 25 restarts). Late ack would trade that for at-least-once delivery we
        # do not want here: a half-executed suite re-run is worse than a failed one,
        # and the run row is already driven to a terminal state by the
        # `task_failure` handler below.
        task_acks_late=False,
        # Celery-beat schedule. The orchestration polling fallback (#171) runs
        # every 10 min as the success channel for runs that produced no webhook;
        # the task looks back further than the interval so nothing slips the gap.
        # Beat runs embedded in the dev worker (`worker -B`); prod uses a separate
        # beat process.
        # Gap recovery (B2) sweeps a wider 1-hour window every 30 min (plus once
        # on beat startup, via the beat_init signal below) to re-ingest runs
        # missed while the system was down — idempotent with the 10-min poll.
        beat_schedule={
            "poll-orchestration-runs": {
                "task": "poll_orchestration_runs",
                "schedule": 600.0,  # 10 minutes
            },
            "recover-orchestration-gaps": {
                "task": "recover_orchestration_gaps",
                "schedule": 1800.0,  # 30 minutes
            },
            # Scheduled suite runs (A7): tick every minute, fire schedules whose
            # precomputed next_run_at has passed. Minute granularity matches the
            # finest standard cron resolution; the task is a cheap indexed scan
            # when nothing is due.
            "dispatch-due-schedules": {
                "task": "dispatch_due_schedules",
                "schedule": 60.0,  # 1 minute
            },
            # Result retention sweep: once a day, scrub `sample_failures` (the only
            # potentially-PII result column) from results past the configured
            # retention window. Keeps the row + `metric_value` so dashboard trends
            # survive (ADR 0012); this is PII minimisation, not a history delete.
            "purge-sample-failures": {
                "task": "purge_sample_failures",
                "schedule": 86400.0,  # 24 hours
            },
            # Stuck-run reaper (#309): every 10 min, fail runs orphaned in a
            # non-terminal state past `stuck_run_threshold_minutes` (a run committed
            # `queued` before `send_task`, or left `running` by a dead worker). The
            # detection threshold (default 60 min) far exceeds the 10-min cadence, so
            # the sweep interval only bounds detection latency, not false reaps.
            "reap-stuck-runs": {
                "task": "reap_stuck_runs",
                "schedule": 600.0,  # 10 minutes
            },
            # Orphan-asset sweep (#770, ADR 0034): once a day (same cadence as the
            # sample-failures retention sweep — this is a low-urgency accretion
            # cleanup, not a liveness janitor), delete `assets` rows whose
            # last_seen is frozen past `asset_orphan_retention_days` AND that no
            # suite/run/lineage_edge still references.
            "sweep-orphan-assets": {
                "task": "sweep_orphan_assets",
                "schedule": 86400.0,  # 24 hours
            },
            # Orphan-SECRET sweep (#1059): once a day, reconcile the secret store
            # against the rows that should own its entries. Daily and low-urgency for
            # the same reason as the asset sweep — and REPORTING-ONLY unless
            # SECRET_ORPHAN_PURGE is set, because the thing it would delete is a live
            # warehouse credential.
            "sweep-orphan-secrets": {
                "task": "sweep_orphan_secrets",
                "schedule": 86400.0,  # 24 hours
            },
            # Catalog lineage pull (#762, ADR 0034): once a day, pull lineage from the
            # configured `LineageProvider` (Marquez) into the `lineage_edges` cache.
            # Dark by default — the task no-ops (zero queries) unless LINEAGE_PROVIDER
            # is set. Daily, not a liveness interval: a cache refresh of external truth
            # whose freshness is deliberately bounded by the catalog's own cadence.
            "refresh-lineage-pull": {
                "task": "refresh_lineage_pull",
                "schedule": 86400.0,  # 24 hours
            },
            # Beat liveness heartbeat (#904): every minute, a task whose only job is
            # to prove the beat→broker→worker loop still EXECUTES. The watchdog
            # thread reads its stamp and exits the process when it goes stale, so a
            # worker that is up but consuming nothing gets restarted instead of
            # silently stopping every scheduled task for hours.
            "beat-heartbeat": {
                "task": "beat_heartbeat",
                "schedule": 60.0,  # 1 minute
            },
            # Warehouse-native lineage refresh (#858, ADR 0034): once a day, pull lineage
            # for every Snowflake / Unity Catalog connection straight from the warehouse's
            # own lineage views into `lineage_edges`. Dark by default — no-ops (zero
            # queries) unless WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_ENABLED. Same low-urgency daily cadence as
            # the catalog pull: a cache refresh of external truth, freshness bounded by the
            # warehouse view's own latency, not a liveness interval.
            "refresh-warehouse-lineage": {
                "task": "refresh_warehouse_lineage",
                "schedule": 86400.0,  # 24 hours
            },
            # Credential-expiry refresh (#838): once a day, re-read the stated
            # expiry of every stored credential that has one (an Azure SAS prints
            # `se=`) into `connections.credential_expires_at`, so the product can
            # warn BEFORE a credential dies rather than after it breaks something.
            # Daily because an expiry date moves only on a rotation, and the
            # warning window is measured in weeks — a cache refresh, not a
            # liveness interval.
            "refresh-credential-expiry": {
                "task": "refresh_credential_expiry",
                "schedule": 86400.0,  # 24 hours
            },
        },
    )
    # Register task modules on worker boot (looks for backend.app.worker.tasks).
    app.autodiscover_tasks(["backend.app.worker"])
    return app

_ON_BEAT_START = (
    # Catches runs that completed while the system was down; the 30-min beat alone
    # would leave that window unswept until its first tick (B2).
    "recover_orchestration_gaps",
    # Populates `credential_expires_at` for credentials that state one (#1024).
    # Its schedule is DAILY, which is right for a value that only moves on a
    # rotation — but wrong for a cold start: a freshly deployed instance, or any
    # connection whose credential predates #838, shows NULL until the first tick.
    # NULL renders as "nothing expires soon", which is indistinguishable from

    # for up to 24h. Prod had exactly this: every connection NULL after the

    # the token.
    "refresh_credential_expiry",
)


@beat_init.connect  # type: ignore[untyped-decorator]  # celery signal .connect is unannotated
def _dispatch_startup_tasks(**_kwargs: Any) -> None:
    """Kick the one-off startup tasks when the beat scheduler starts.

    Tied to ``beat_init`` (one beat process per deployment) rather than worker
    boot, so each fires **once** per restart instead of once per worker — no
    thundering herd of identical sweeps on a multi-worker deploy. Enqueued by name
    (decoupled from the task module) to the broker so a ready worker runs them.

    Best-effort and **independently guarded**: a broker hiccup at startup must not
    crash beat, and one task failing to enqueue must not skip the rest (the
    schedule recovers shortly either way).
    """
    log = get_logger(__name__)
    for name in _ON_BEAT_START:
        try:
            celery_app.send_task(name)
        except Exception:  # pragma: no cover - defensive; startup must not fail on broker
            log.exception("startup_task_dispatch_failed", task=name)


@worker_ready.connect  # type: ignore[untyped-decorator]  # celery signal .connect is unannotated
def _start_beat_watchdog(**_kwargs: Any) -> None:
    """Arm the beat liveness watchdog once this worker is consuming (#904).

    Hooked on ``worker_ready`` (the main process, after the pool is up) rather
    than ``worker_process_init`` (which fires in every prefork CHILD — N children
    would mean N watchdogs racing to kill the same process, and a child's exit
    would not restart the container anyway).

    The watchdog reads the heartbeat the ``beat_heartbeat`` task writes on
    execution and exits the process when it goes stale, so the platform restarts
    a worker that is up but consuming nothing (#904/#905). Best-effort: it must

def warehouse_lineage_status(session: Session) -> list[WarehouseLineageStatus]:
    """Warehouse-native lineage sources that are degraded or failing (#858 slice 4).

    Workspace-wide (like `failing_lineage_sources`): a warehouse's lineage tier is a
    property of the source, not the asset. Lists only Snowflake / Unity Catalog
    connections that have refreshed at least once AND are either degraded (a coarser
    tier — e.g. Snowflake OBJECT_DEPENDENCIES because the account isn't Enterprise) or
    errored (the last refresh failed). A healthy full-tier source is omitted — no banner
    over a clean, current graph.
    """
    rows = session.scalars(
        select(Connection).where(
            Connection.type.in_(("snowflake", "unity_catalog")),
            Connection.lineage_last_refresh_at.is_not(None),
            or_(
                Connection.lineage_degraded_reason.is_not(None),
                Connection.lineage_last_error.is_not(None),
            ),
        )
    ).all()
    return [
        WarehouseLineageStatus(
            connection_id=c.id,
            name=c.name,
            type=c.type,
            tier=c.lineage_last_tier,
            degraded_reason=c.lineage_degraded_reason,
            last_error=c.lineage_last_error,
            last_refreshed_at=c.lineage_last_refresh_at,
        )
        for c in rows
    ]


def failing_lineage_sources(session: Session) -> list[LineageSourceHealth]:
    """Lineage-feeding connections whose poll is currently failing (#828).

    Workspace-wide, not per-asset, and deliberately so: lineage arrives from a *source*
    (a dbt project's manifest), not from the asset. If that source is down, every asset's
    lineage is suspect — including the ones that legitimately have none — so the caveat
    belongs on all of them.

    Scoped to `dbt` because it is the only orchestration provider that feeds lineage
    today (`read_manifest`, #759). Widening it means adding a provider, not rewriting
    this: the filter rides the existing capability, not a hardcoded list of names.
    """
    rows = session.scalars(
        select(Connection).where(
            Connection.type == "dbt",
            Connection.consecutive_poll_failures > 0,
        )
    ).all()
    return [
        LineageSourceHealth(
            connection_id=c.id,
            name=c.name,
            type=c.type,
            consecutive_failures=c.consecutive_poll_failures,
            last_error=c.last_poll_error,
            last_polled_at=c.last_polled_at,
        )
        for c in rows
    ]

def get_lineage_provider() -> LineageProvider | None:
    """The configured `LineageProvider`, or ``None`` when unconfigured (dark by default).

    Reads typed ``Settings`` (``lineage_provider`` + ``marquez_url``) — the emitter's
    gate pattern — so a value in ``.env.app`` (which the process env never sees)
    activates the pull. ``lineage_provider`` unset → ``None`` (no pull). An unknown
    provider name, or ``marquez`` without a URL, logs a warning and returns ``None``.
    """
    settings = get_settings()
    name = (settings.lineage_provider or "").strip().lower()

        return MarquezLineageProvider(settings.marquez_url)
    log.warning("lineage_provider_unknown", provider=name)
